Summary: The paper compares generation strategies for writing OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited, holding one model (Claude Opus 5.5), the supplied sources, the guards, a claim-level audit and the scoring fixed. The benchmark has 100 entries with 2-12 references (515 papers; 96, or 19%, readable in full via open access). The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', scores what a draft says about each cited paper against 6,652 atomic facts split once, without sight of any draft, from OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs as deposited in ClinVar; synopsis HPO terms, variants, causal gene and inheritance are secondary. The strategies are direct reading of all papers in one prompt, an agentic curator, an evidence graph, a case table, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control and three add-ons. Main findings: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries; +43.7 points, 95% CI 38.3 to 49.1; Table 24); on the 93 entries every strategy completed, the agent and the evidence graph are 0.6 and 0.5 points below direct reading and the case table 1.9 below (-3.1 to -0.8; sign test p = 0.071; Table 1), with orderings that change with the entry set and, for the case table, extraction settings (Appendix F); on 38 held-out entries a completeness pass adds 2.6 points (1.7 to 3.6) while drafts grow from 10,802 to 14,412 characters (Sec. 4.3); and a planted-error test shows the audit catches citation swaps and single-value substitutions but not added citations (best-verdict rule) or omissions (Sec. 4.5). All judgements come from the writer's model family and none was validated by a person. The three reviewers agree that the design is unusually careful and transparent, and that the paper is held back by the unvalidated same-family judge, a single model whose safety filter shapes the compared sets, a near-ceiling regime in which designs can differ by only a few points, a recall-only endpoint confounded with draft length, a reference others cannot reuse, and dense presentation. All three score it 5 (Reject, confidence 4). The reviewers name expert validation of a stratified sample of judgements (with a cross-family re-judging of the existing drafts) as the central missing piece, followed by a length-controlled view of the reading-better gains and a main text whose headline claims are scoped to the regime tested.
Strengths: Careful control of confounds that most system comparisons leave open: one model, the curators' own reference lists, shared guards, one audit and one scoring procedure, so differences can be attributed to the strategy (Sec. 3, Fig. 1). The access manipulation is within-paper (the same papers given as full text or as abstracts to the same writer on the same entries and facts; Sec. 4.1, Table 24), which turns an otherwise observational and confounded access breakdown (Tables 13-14) into a clean paired comparison: full text is better on 45 of 46 entries and tied on one.

Strong experimental hygiene for an LLM-pipeline comparison: fact lists split once without sight of any draft (Sec. 3.3); paired bootstrap intervals over entries, better/worse/tied counts and exact sign tests, Holm-adjusted on the secondary measures (Tables 7-8; the reported sign-test p-values reproduce from the counts); judge re-runs and run-to-run replicates that give an explicit noise yardstick (1.0-point half-width over 93 entries; App. E, Table 20); an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 11); and a matched ablation separating settings from paradigm (Table 21).

Exemplary transparency about the status of each analysis. Every experiment's status, entry set and dropouts are tabulated (Tables 2-3); all nine post hoc choices are listed (Sec. 3.3 (a)-(i)), including that the symmetric completion rule was adopted after a first analysis put the evidence graph 2.1 points behind (App. M.4).

Safety-filter stops are treated as a measured outcome rather than silently retried: the symmetric rule (a stopped reply costs a one-call strategy the whole entry but a per-paper strategy one paper), completion tables, and sensitivity analyses that show the choice can change conclusions (Sec. 3.3; Tables 5, 11, 29, 32, 55). This is a practical lesson for anyone benchmarking multi-call pipelines.

The decomposition of coverage by whether the supplied text states each fact (Fig. 2b-c, Table 19, Fig. 6) is a useful diagnostic: reading strategies convey 91.0-94.4% of stated facts and 5.5-6.9% of unstated ones, no better than the memory-only control (8.2%), which locates the headroom for reading better (about 4% of facts; Sec. 4.1) and the case table's deficit (-8.4 points on stated full-text facts; Fig. 3a).

The audit stress test gives concrete, mechanistically explained blind spots that practitioners can act on: under best-verdict aggregation none of 30 added irrelevant citations was flagged although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for all 176 claims attributed to it; omissions are invisible by construction; deleted qualifiers were caught in 11 of 30 items, with no zygosity or 'one family' deletion caught (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4, Tables 50-53). The paper states plainly that the audit checks fidelity, not correctness or completeness.

A memory-only control by creation era and on entries created in 2026 (Fig. 5, Tables 15-16, 55; App. M.2) is a sensible, if partial, contamination check: memory-only coverage falls to 5.7% in the newest band and 7.0% on the 2026 entries, where direct reading stays near 52%. Cost, calls, tokens and draft length are reported beside quality (Tables 12, 34), and drafts, verdicts and per-entry scores are to be released.
Weaknesses: No person validated any judgement. Fact splitting, the present/partly/absent/contradicted marks, the 'stated in the supplied text' label and the audit verdicts all come from the writer's model family (Sec. 3.2-3.3; Limitation (i)); the 95.7% agreement between two judgings (App. E) shows self-consistency only. The 43.7-point access effect is too large to be a judge artefact, but the 0.5-3-point strategy and reading-better differences (Tables 1, 30) are the size that self-preference, style bias or correlated errors between the 'stated' and 'conveyed' judgements could produce, and extract-then-write drafts are longer (113.5 and 117.9 vs 101.0 audited claims per entry; Table 1). For a paper whose main contribution is a benchmark and a measurement, an expert-labelled stratified sample (a few hundred facts by access level and status, with chance-corrected agreement and attention to 'partly present' and 'not stated') and a re-judging of the existing drafts by a judge from another model family are the central missing pieces.

One proprietary model, run through a command-line interface without temperature or seed control, writes, audits and judges (Sec. 3.2, App. B); whether the access effect and the order of strategies transfer to other writers, notably smaller-context ones where one-prompt reading is impossible, is untested (Limitation (ii)). Its safety filter removed entries unevenly and in a content-correlated way: 7 of 100 main entries (Table 5); 10 of 30 entries created in 2026, every one a case-table per-paper failure, with 6 agentic-curator drafts also lost (Table 55); at least one strategy on each of the 4 large entries (Table 49); and all 30 of STORM's research prompts (Table 37). The three entries the completeness pass lost are exactly the three where the evidence graph lost a paper (Tables 5, 29). Comparing only completed entries conditions on a post-treatment outcome: under intention to treat the agent's difference changes sign (-0.6 to +0.4) and the case table's interval includes zero (Table 11), and counting a stopped revision as zero turns the completeness-pass and combined-arm gains of +2.4 and +3.1 into -3.5 and -4.8 on the mean (Table 32). Keeping the unrevised draft is a reasonable design choice, not a measured property of the arm, and the abstract's +2.6 should carry that dependence.

The strategy comparison runs in a near-ceiling regime with little room for designs to separate: 2-12 references that fit one prompt, 81% of papers readable only as abstract or title, reading strategies conveying 91.0-94.4% of stated facts, and about 4% of all facts stated but not fully conveyed (Sec. 4.1; Table 19, where 58-59 of 79 entries tie on stated abstract-only facts for the agent and the graph). The regimes where agents or intermediate representations should help were not evaluated: no large entry was completed by every strategy (App. K.2), the 30-75-reference tier reports no findings (App. M.1), and padding used unrelated papers that no draft cited, so it tests input size rather than crowding (App. K.1). Sec. 5 concedes that the regime favours direct reading, but the abstract, Sec. 1 and the Conclusion state that designs 'differ by a few points either way' without that restriction (and at the main settings no design was ahead of direct reading; the 'either way' rests on post hoc subsets).

The parity message is informal. The paper rightly makes no equivalence claim because no margin was set (Sec. 4.2), yet the conclusion reads as parity; the intervals for the agent (-1.3 to 0.0) and the graph (-1.5 to +0.5) exclude neither a small deficit nor a small advantage. An equivalence test against a margin justified by curation needs or by the replicate-noise yardstick of 1.0 point (App. E) would make the claim testable.

Paradigm-level statements rest on one prompt-level implementation per paradigm (Limitation (iii)), and these implementations move with settings and entry set by as much as the between-design differences: matched settings move the case table by +2.1 points (Table 21); the evidence graph is -1.2 on the ablation's 19 entries with half or more full text and +3.1 on the other 19, on the same drafts (App. F); and it is ahead of direct reading in all three replicates on the 30-entry subset but -0.5 on the 93 entries (App. E). The released-pipeline comparison does not fill the gap: 10 and 4 entries, PaperQA2 without its agent, STORM with no article, and six concatenated question answers against one-pass entry writing, which confounds protocol with design (App. J, Tables 35-43). App. J's statement that the study's implementations 'are thus not outperformed by released pipelines' is stronger than this design supports.

The primary endpoint is recall-only and narrow. It scores only variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs (327 of 515 papers have one; Sec. 3.1); about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in it (App. H); and synopsis exact F1 is about 34-36% for every reading strategy (Table 1), with 1,835 of the 2,311 HPO annotations coming from HPO's own curation (Sec. 3.1). The reading-better gains come with longer drafts (completeness pass: 10,802 to 14,412 characters and 129 to 164 checkable claims per audited entry; Tables 33-34); the three-draft merge's +3.1 includes +1.5 on facts the text does not state (Table 30), with 95.8% of claims supported and variant precision 83.4% against 87.1% (Tables 33-34). The only precision-side check is the audit on 20 entries without intervals (Table 33). Without a length-matched baseline (for example direct reading asked for about 14,000 characters, or drafts truncated to baseline length) or a length-normalised or precision-paired endpoint, 'reading more completely recovers a few points' is not separated from 'writing more recovers a few points'.

Much of the evidence rests on choices made after results were seen. Two apply to every result: fixed fact lists replacing per-draft splitting, and the symmetric completion rule, adopted after a first analysis put the evidence graph 2.1 points behind (Sec. 3.3 (a)-(b); App. M.4). The case table's clearest deficit (-8.4 points on stated full-text facts; Fig. 3a, Table 19), the matched ablation and the fourth reading-better arm are post hoc; the main strategies were developed on their own evaluation entries (Limitation (ix)); only the 20 compared 2026 entries and the reading-better split are held out; and no registered or time-stamped protocol is cited, so pre-specification cannot be verified externally. The labelling is exemplary, but the confirmatory core is an essentially null main comparison, an expected access effect and three prompt-level arms.

Memorisation is not excluded as a contributor to the reading results. The causal gene is withheld, yet memory alone names it with F1 88.9-100% in the four older bands (Table 16). Within abstract-only papers, direct reading's pooled coverage is highest in the 600000-609999 band (49.8%), where memory-only coverage also peaks (22.9%), and falls to 37.9% in the newest band (Table 15); 10.0% of partly conveyed abstract-only facts are stated in no supplied text (Sec. 4.1). The paper notes the pattern but does not analyse it (Sec. 4.2), and the clean held-out check is 20 entries (App. M.2).

The benchmark cannot be reused as released. The fixed fact lists carry curator wording and are not redistributed; a rebuilt reference must be split again, and how much a fresh split by the same procedure moves levels and paired differences was not measured, while per-draft splitting already ran 2-5 points higher (Sec. 3.1 'Reuse'; Table 6; Ethics and Reproducibility statements). Third parties therefore cannot score a new strategy on the reported denominators, which weakens contribution (1), a benchmark harness whose motivation is comparison with sources and scoring held fixed.

The audit stress test is small and selected: 30 items per class, planted only in evidence-graph paragraphs that had already passed the audit, with controls that had passed once, so no specificity estimate for arbitrary paragraphs exists (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4, App. L). The obvious alternative to best-verdict aggregation, flagging a claim when any cited paper fails it, was not evaluated (Sec. 4.5), although the stored per-(claim, paper) verdicts for 78-88 replayable entries per strategy (Table 53) would give its flag rate without new generation.

Novelty and significance for an ICLR audience are modest. No new method is proposed (Sec. 2), the strategies are prompt-level instances of known designs, and the main findings are largely predictable: the reference consists of variant paragraphs curators wrote from full papers, and the supplied text states 76% of facts about full-text papers but 26% about abstract-only papers (1,246 of 1,639 and 1,099 of 4,221; Table 19), so the access contrast largely measures how much of the reference abstracts contain, which the paper itself calls 'expected' (Sec. 1); likewise an attribution audit cannot see omissions, and best-verdict aggregation hides over-citation. The careful measurement is the contribution, but its reach is limited by the single model, the unvalidated judge and the non-redistributable reference, and it may fit a datasets-and-benchmarks or bioinformatics venue better.

Presentation is very dense. The ten-page body is a sequence of hedged numerical statements; terms with local meanings ('held out', 'no arm repaired', 'stopped', 'completion') appear in the abstract and Sec. 1 before Sec. 3.3 defines them; Tables 2-55 in about 40 appendix pages carry much of the substance; there is no worked example (curator paragraph, fixed fact list, draft paragraph, per-fact judgement and audit verdict) and no prompt in the paper, so what a 'fact' or 'partly present' is cannot be seen; secondary threads (add-ons, released systems, padding, large entries) compete with the core story; and the long title states no finding. Two main-text summaries also need correcting: the hidden-full-text fact set is undefined (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a and Table 24 do not say whether the 136 paragraphs and 2,120 facts are only those about the 91 hidden papers, and the counts do not match Table 13's access classification), and Sec. 4.4's 'cost no strategy more than about a point' omits that direct reading gained 3.2-3.6 points under padding, so the other three fell 2.8-4.6 points behind it at about 500,000 characters with intervals excluding zero (Table 46, interaction; 6 entries).
Questions: Can you add a human validation on a stratified sample, for example 200-300 fixed facts judged present/partly/absent and stated/not stated by two clinical geneticists, with Cohen's kappa against the model judges, reported separately by access level and for facts on which strategies disagree? Would the 0.5-3-point strategy and reading-better differences survive the observed disagreement rate?

Re-judging needs no new generation: does a judge from another model family, applied to the existing drafts and fixed fact lists (all 93 entries, or at least the 30 replicate entries), reproduce the order of strategies and the sign of the case-table deficit? Can one other writer test whether the 43.7-point access effect and the strategy order hold?

In the hidden-full-text experiment, are the 136 paragraphs and 2,120 facts restricted to paragraphs about the 91 hidden papers, and how are the facts of a paragraph that cites several papers assigned an access level? Table 13 counts 1,639 full-text-paper facts in 40 of the 93 compared entries, and the 7 excluded entries hold only 413 facts, so at most 2,052 facts in all 100 entries are full-text-paper facts by that classification, fewer than 2,120; and 49 entries have an in-scope paragraph about a full-text paper (Sec. 4.1), so at least 42 of the 93 should have such facts. Please define the set and report the contrast on facts about the hidden papers alone.

For the reading-better arms, what is coverage per 1,000 characters or at matched length (drafts truncated to the baseline's length per paper), and what does a length-matched control give (direct reading asked for about 14,000 characters, or a second unrevised sample appended without merging)? Can the precision-side check be extended beyond 20 entries, with intervals?

With the existing per-entry differences, what does an equivalence test (TOST) conclude for the agent and the evidence graph at a margin of 2 points and at the 1.0-point replicate yardstick, and how would you justify a margin in curation terms?

How much does an independent second split of the curator paragraphs by the same procedure move levels and paired differences (for example, the 30 replicate entries split twice)? Could you release per-fact identifiers with hashes of the fact text, or reach an agreement with the rights holder, so that groups with licensed access can verify they rebuilt the same denominators?

Using the stored per-(claim, paper) verdicts behind Table 53, how many claims in real drafts would an 'any cited paper fails' rule flag, and how many of those are true over-citations on a small manual check?

Of the 111 (evidence graph) and 130 (case table) generated variants that OMIM does not list (Table 10), what share does the audit find supported by the cited papers? The current precision definition counts these as misses, which may penalise thorough extraction.

Can the era pattern in direct reading's abstract-only coverage (Table 15) be tested for memory, for example by comparing coverage on facts the memory-only draft also conveys with facts it does not, by band?

Are safety-filter stops concentrated in particular disease areas, paper types or input lengths, and does excluding the 7 incomplete main entries shift the compared set? Did you consider a pre-specified sensitivity analysis that sends only the stopped calls to a neutral rewording or a second model?
Are the paired differences and intervals of Table 1 stable when 'partly present' receives no credit, as the levels are in Table 6?

What kinds of facts does the case table lose on stated full-text facts (-8.4 points; Fig. 3a): does its per-patient schema drop functional-study or non-patient variant findings? Why is the evidence graph ahead on full-text facts (+1.2) but behind on abstract facts (-1.9) in Table 13?

Since the agentic curator's tool calls are not logged and paper opening is self-reported (App. B), how confident can one be that it read every paper? Is GraphRAG global search's 20.5% coverage of facts the text does not state (Table 36) an artefact of the looser community-report citation mapping or recalled content?
Limitations: The authors' limitations (Sec. 5 (i)-(xii) and the Ethics statement) are thorough, specific and candid. The unresolved main threats to the conclusions are the absence of any human-labelled validation of the judges, of any second model family as writer or judge, and of a fresh-split stability measurement for anyone rebuilding the reference.

The practical takeaway (access matters more than strategy) is specific to a variant-centred endpoint, to entries with 2-12 references whose papers fit one prompt and are mostly abstracts, and to one model whose safety filter removes entries non-randomly (including all large entries and STORM). These boundaries should be stated in the abstract and conclusion, not only in Sec. 5.

The primary endpoint is recall-only, has no length or precision counterpart, covers only the variant-centred part of an entry and about a quarter of what drafts say; conclusions about writing full knowledge-base entries extend beyond what it measures.

The reference cannot be redistributed, so others cannot reproduce the scoring denominators. Memorisation of public OMIM content is not ruled out for older entries; the held-out 2026 check covers 20 entries.

The audit checks fidelity to the cited text, not correctness or completeness, and is blind to over-citation and omissions; the planted-error study is small (30 items per class) and exploratory. Given the clinical-genetics setting, a sentence on automation bias is warranted: reviewers may over-trust audited drafts when omissions and over-citation go undetected. The statement that generated drafts are not clinical guidance and must be marked as machine generated, not as OMIM content, is appropriate.
